title: Healthy food and drink: why we need water, and where it hides

summary.text: Squeeze a piece of cucumber in a clean hanky, and drops of water run out. Squeeze a biscuit, and nothing comes. Your body needs food to grow and move, and water every single day. Your child finds out which foods hold water inside, and why we feel thirsty. They also find out that liking a food can change, one small taste at a time.
summary.art: A child's hands twisting a white hanky over a small glass, with drops falling in, and a row of foods on a steel plate: cucumber, watermelon, banana, biscuit.

intro.hook: Hold a piece of cucumber in one hand and a biscuit in the other. Both feel dry on the outside. Is there water hiding inside either of them?
intro.text: Your body needs water every day. You drink it from a tumbler. But some water also comes in your food. Which foods carry water inside them? Which carry almost none? In this unit we squeeze foods to find out. We also ask why we feel thirsty, and why we like some foods more than others.
intro.art: A child holding a cucumber slice in one hand and a biscuit in the other, looking from one to the other.

outcomes: By the end I can say why my body needs food and water: to grow, to move and to stay well.
By the end I can say that my body loses water all day, so I need to drink every day.
By the end I can show which foods have water inside them, by squeezing them.
By the end I can say that I may learn to like a food by tasting it many times.
By the end I can say why lots of sweet food and drink is hard on my teeth.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw.

terms.meaning: Healthy means your body is well and strong, and can grow, play and mend.
terms.example: Fruit, vegetables, dal, rice, eggs, milk and water help keep you healthy.
terms.art: A child running happily across a room, with a tumbler of water and a plate of rice, dal and vegetables on the table.

terms.meaning: You are thirsty when your body needs water. Your mouth feels dry and you want a drink.
terms.example: After playing in the hot sun, you come home thirsty.
terms.art: A hot, red-cheeked child coming in from the balcony and reaching for a steel tumbler of water.

terms.meaning: Sweat is water that comes out through your skin. It helps your body cool down.
terms.example: On a hot day in Chennai, sweat makes your forehead wet.
terms.art: A child's forehead with small drops of sweat, and a bright sun outside the window.

terms.meaning: Taste is what your tongue tells you about food: sweet, sour, salty or bitter.
terms.example: Jaggery tastes sweet. Tamarind tastes sour. Karela tastes bitter.
terms.art: A child's tongue poking out, with a lump of jaggery, a piece of tamarind and a slice of karela beside it.

explanations.concept: Food and drink keep us healthy
explanations.definition: Food gives your body what it needs to grow, to move and to mend itself. Water helps every part of your body work.
explanations.description: Your body is always busy. It grows taller, mends a scraped knee and lets you run. All of this needs food. Eat many kinds: rice or ragi, dal, vegetables, fruit, curd or milk, and eggs or fish if your family eats them. Lots of sweet food is hard on your teeth.
examples: A plate of rice, sambar, a vegetable and curd gives many kinds of food at once.
A scraped knee heals in about a week, and your body uses food to build the new skin.
Kamala Sohonie, a scientist from India, found vitamins in neera, the sweet sap of palm trees. She said it could be a cheap, healthy drink for children who did not get enough food.
explanations.context: This card says why we need food and drink.
explanations.art: A banana-leaf meal with rice, sambar, a vegetable, curd and a tumbler of water, with a child's healed knee in the corner.

explanations.concept: Your body needs water every day
explanations.definition: More than half of your body is water. You lose some all day, so you need to drink every day.
explanations.description: Your blood is mostly water. Water leaves your body all day: as sweat through your skin, in your breath, and when you wee. When your body is short of water, a part of your brain notices, and you feel thirsty. Thirst is your body asking for a drink.
examples: After a game in the sun, your T-shirt is wet with sweat, and you feel thirsty.
In summer in Hyderabad or Nagpur, children need to drink more than in the cool months.
When you breathe onto a cold window, it mists up. That mist is water from your breath.
explanations.context: This card says why we drink water every day.
explanations.art: A simple drawing of a child with blue arrows: water going in from a tumbler, and coming out as sweat on the skin and mist from the mouth.

explanations.concept: Some water comes in your food
explanations.definition: Most foods have some water inside them. Some foods, like cucumber and watermelon, are mostly water.
explanations.description: A cucumber is about 95 parts water out of every 100. The cucumber plant drank that water through their roots and kept it in the fruit. Cooked rice, dal and idli hold water too, because water is used to cook them. Dry foods, like biscuits, roasted chana and murmura, hold almost none.
examples: Cucumber and watermelon drip water when you squeeze them.
Dry rice grains are hard. Cooked rice is soft, because the grains took in water in the pot.
A biscuit stays dry when you squeeze it. If you dip it in milk, it soaks the milk up.
explanations.context: This card says where water hides in our food. It goes with the squeeze test.
explanations.art: A cucumber cut open, with tiny drops on the cut face, next to a bowl of cooked rice and a heap of dry murmura.

explanations.concept: Why we like the foods we like
explanations.description: Babies are born liking sweet tastes and pulling a face at bitter ones. But liking is also learned. Many children push away a new food at first, and come to like it after many small tastes. Scientists are still finding out how much of liking is born in us, and how much is learned.
examples: A baby smiles at a drop of something sweet, and screws up their face at something bitter.
Many children who disliked karela or pavakkai come to enjoy it when they are older.
Some people find that coriander leaves taste like soap. This seems to be partly because of how their bodies are made.

perspectives.explanation: Liking sweet and disliking bitter is there from birth. Sweet foods usually carry energy, and many bitter things in nature can make you ill.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how children learn to eat, like Leann Birch
perspectives.explanation: Most likes are learned. Children come to like the foods they taste many times, without being pushed.
We learn to enjoy many tastes together. On Ugadi, families in Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana eat a pachadi with sweet, sour, salty, bitter and hot tastes in one spoonful.

explanations.context: This card is about the foods we like, and why our likes can change.
explanations.art: A small child tasting a tiny piece of karela with a thoughtful face, while a grown-up smiles at her.

agreed.text: Every person needs to drink water every day.
agreed.evidence: Water leaves the body all the time, in sweat, breath and wee. Doctors everywhere see that people who go without water become ill within days.

agreed.text: Eating many kinds of food, with plenty of vegetables and fruit, helps keep a body healthy.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have followed what large numbers of people eat for many years. People who eat many kinds of food, with plenty of vegetables and fruit, tend to stay healthier.

agreed.text: Sugar on your teeth for a long time can make holes in them.
agreed.evidence: Tiny living beings called bacteria live in every mouth. They feed on sugar and make an acid that wears away teeth. Dentists see more holes in the teeth of people who eat sweet things often.

challenging.claim: Everyone must drink exactly 8 glasses of water every day.
challenging.who: A popular rule, often printed in magazines
challenging.for: Our bodies do need water every day, and many people forget to drink.
challenging.against: How much water a person needs depends on their size, the weather and how much they run about. Some water also comes in food. Doctors have found no proof for one exact number for everyone. Drinking when you feel thirsty, and more on hot days, works well for most healthy children.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular rule for drinking water.

challenging.claim: Sweets make children wild and jumpy.
challenging.who: A very common belief among parents
challenging.for: Children are often wild at parties, where there are lots of sweets.
challenging.against: Scientists tested this carefully. Some children got sugar and some did not, and nobody knew who got which. Their behaviour was the same. Parties are exciting, sweets or no sweets. Sweets are still hard on teeth.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief about sweets.

challenging.claim: If a child does not like a food the first time, they will never like it.
challenging.for: Many children make a face and push away a new food.
challenging.against: Leann Birch and other scientists found that many children come to like a food after tasting it many times. Pushing a child to eat it can make them like it less.
challenging.context: This card is about whether our likes can change.

big_questions.q: The water in a cucumber came from rain, through the cucumber plant's roots. When you eat the cucumber, whose water is it?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the water was before the plant drank it, and where the water goes after it leaves you.

big_questions.q: How does your body know it is short of water, before you even think about it?
big_questions.hint: Your body senses many things without asking you. Where do you feel thirst?

big_questions.q: If you can learn to like karela, are your likes really yours?
big_questions.hint: Think of a food you liked when you were small, and one you like now.

big_questions.q: Every living being on Earth needs water. What would the world be like with no water at all?
big_questions.hint: Think of plants, crows, ants, fish and you.

story.title: Cucumbers at the Station
story.note: Kavya, Arjun and their mother are made up. Cucumber really is about 95% water, and cucumber slices with salt and chilli really are sold at many Indian railway stations.
text: Kavya was six. She lived in Chennai with her mother and her little brother, Arjun, who was four. One hot day in May, the three of them took the train to visit their grandmother, Paati, in Madurai.
Amma had filled a big steel bottle with water. Kavya drank some. Arjun drank some. Then Arjun drank some more, and some more. By the time the train stopped at a big station, the bottle was empty.
'I'm thirsty,' said Arjun. His cheeks were pink. His hair was stuck to his forehead with sweat. 'I'm so thirsty, Amma.'
'We will buy water here,' said Amma. She looked out of the window. The water seller was at the far end of the platform, with a long line of people waiting. The train would leave in a few minutes.

Just then a woman walked past the window with a basket on her head. 'Vellarikkai! Vellarikkai!' she called. In her basket were long, green cucumbers. She cut them into slices and sprinkled them with salt and red chilli powder.
Amma bought a paper cone of cucumber slices. Kavya took a slice and bit it. It was cold and crunchy. Juice ran down her chin.
Kavya looked at the slice in her hand. She squeezed it between her fingers. Drops of water fell onto her frock. She squeezed again. More drops.
'Arjun,' she said. 'Look. The cucumber is full of water.'
Arjun did not believe her. So Kavya held a slice over his open hand and squeezed it hard. Three cool drops fell into his palm. Arjun stared at them. Then he licked them up.
'It tastes like water,' he said, surprised. 'Water with a bit of cucumber.'
'It is mostly water,' said Kavya. 'The cucumber plant drank the water from the ground. Now the water is in the cucumber. So if you eat the cucumber, you get the water too.'
Arjun ate one slice. Then another. Then four more. He stopped asking for water. The chilli made his tongue tingle, and he laughed.
'Is a biscuit full of water too?' he asked. Kavya thought about it. She took a biscuit from Amma's bag and squeezed it. It broke into crumbs. Not one drop came out.
'No,' said Kavya. 'Biscuits are dry. Cucumbers are wet.'

At the next station, Amma bought a new bottle of water. 'The cucumber helped,' she said, 'but in this heat, your bodies need a proper drink too.' Arjun and Kavya both drank, slowly, all the way to Madurai.

That night in Madurai, Kavya lay on her mat and thought about all the water in the world. Rain falls into the ground. Plants drink the water. We eat the plants. The water goes into us. Then it comes out again, in our sweat and our breath. She wondered where the water in her cucumber would go next.
story.epiphany: Kavya squeezes a cucumber slice and sees water drip out. She works out that food can carry water inside it, so eating a cucumber also gives you a drink.
ask: Why was Arjun so thirsty on the train?
Kavya squeezed a cucumber and a biscuit. What happened to each one?
Amma still bought water after the cucumbers. Why do you think she did?
art: A crowded, sunny train compartment with a girl at the window bars and a little boy on his mother's lap holding an empty steel bottle.
A woman on a railway platform with a basket of green cucumbers on her head, handing a paper cone of cucumber slices through a train window.
A girl squeezing a cucumber slice over her little brother's open palm, with three drops of water falling.

experiments.title: The Squeeze Test: which foods have water inside?
experiments.context: In this experiment you squeeze small pieces of food in a clean hanky. Some foods drip water. Some stay dry. You guess first, then you find out.
experiments.question: Which foods from our kitchen have water inside them, and which have almost none?
experiments.predict: Look at each food and touch it. Which ones do you think have water inside? Which are dry inside? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each piece of food is about one big spoonful. A grown-up mashes or crushes each one with a fork or the back of a spoon first. We press each one on paper for the same count of ten. We squeeze each one in the same hanky, as hard as we can, and dry the hanky between foods.
results_table: My guess: wet or dry inside?

materials.item: a piece of cucumber, cut into small bits by a grown-up
a piece of watermelon, or an orange segment, or a tomato piece
a piece of ripe banana
cooked rice
a plain biscuit
roasted chana, murmura or pori
a clean, tightly woven cotton hanky or a piece of old cotton cloth
a fork or spoon, for the grown-up to mash the foods
a small see-through glass, or a steel katori
paper napkins, tissue or old newspaper
materials.qty: 12 squares (6 for the paper test, 6 for drying the hanky)

materials.item: a steel plate to lay the foods out on

schedule.what: Guess, then do the paper test and the squeeze test on six foods.

experiments.record: Draw the six foods in a row. Draw drops under each food that dripped. Draw a cross under each food that stayed dry.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Few or no drops, just mush

setup.art: Six small heaps of food in a row on a steel plate: cucumber bits, watermelon, banana, cooked rice, a biscuit and roasted chana.
setup.caption: 1. Put six foods in a row. Guess which are wet inside.

setup.art: A child pressing a piece of cucumber onto a square of paper napkin, with a wet patch showing round it.
setup.caption: 2. Press each food on paper. Count to ten. Look for a wet mark.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child twisting a white hanky with cucumber bits inside over a small glass, with drops falling in.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze each food in the hanky over a glass. Watch for drops.

flow.do: 1. Put the six foods in a row on the steel plate. 2. Let your child touch each food. 3. Ask them to guess which foods are wet inside.
flow.say: Here are six foods. Touch each one. Which ones do you think have water inside? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Touch each food. Which ones have water inside? Guess. Say why.

good: The cucumber feels cold and wet.
The biscuit is crunchy, so it is dry.
The banana is soft, so maybe it has water.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Write each guess down, or put a small piece of paper marked W (wet) or D (dry) next to each food. Many children guess that banana is dry, because it feels dry on the outside.

flow.do: 1. Put six paper squares (napkin, tissue or newspaper) on the table. 2. A grown-up mashes or crushes each food. 3. Spoon each food onto its own square and press. 4. Count to ten together. 5. Lift the food and look at the paper.
flow.say: Press the food down on the paper. Let's count to ten. Now lift it. Is the paper wet?
flow.kid: Press the food on the paper. Count to ten. Lift it. Is the paper wet?

good: The cucumber and watermelon papers got very wet.
The banana made a small damp mark.

flow.parent: Mashed cucumber, watermelon and tomato make a big wet patch. Banana and cooked rice usually make a small damp, sticky mark. The biscuit and chana leave no wet mark.

flow.do: 1. Put the mashed cucumber in the middle of the hanky. 2. Gather the corners and twist them over the glass. 3. Squeeze hard. 4. Pat the hanky dry with a napkin, wipe the glass, and do the same with each food.
flow.say: Now the squeeze test. Hold the hanky over the glass. Twist and squeeze as hard as you can. What comes out?
flow.kid: Put the food in the hanky. Twist it over the glass. Squeeze hard! What comes out?

ask.q: What came out of the cucumber?
good: Lots of drops fell in the glass.

ask.q: What came out of the biscuit?

flow.parent: Small children's hands may not be strong enough, so twist the hanky together. Cucumber and watermelon give clear drops within a few seconds. Squeeze the dry foods last. Pat the hanky dry and wipe the glass between foods, so you can compare the drops.

flow.do: 1. Line up the foods from the one that gave the most water to the one that gave none. 2. Look at the guesses again. 3. Ask your child to say what they found, and what showed it.
flow.say: Which food gave the most water? Which gave none? Was your guess right? What did you see that tells you?
flow.kid: Put the foods in a line, from most water to no water. Was your guess right?

check.q: Which food gave the most water when you squeezed it?
check.why: Cucumber is mostly water. The water runs out when you squeeze it. The biscuit and the chana are dry, so no water came out.

flow.parent: A good answer says what your child found and what showed it, for example 'The cucumber has lots of water inside, because drops came out when I squeezed it.' If your child guessed banana was dry, praise the guess. A banana is about three-quarters water, but holds it tightly in a soft paste, so it does not drip.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they get when they eat a cucumber. 2. Eat the leftover foods together, so nothing is wasted.
flow.say: So when you eat a cucumber, what does your body get? Now let's eat our test foods.
flow.kid: What do you get when you eat cucumber? Now eat the foods!

ask.q: What does your body get when you eat a cucumber?

flow.parent: Keep the squeezed foods for eating only if the hanky and hands were clean. Otherwise eat the leftover unsqueezed pieces.

activities.title: The Feely Bag: guess the fruit or vegetable
activities.context: In this activity you put your hand into a cloth bag and feel a fruit or vegetable you cannot see. You guess what it is by touch.

materials.item: a cloth bag, a pillow cover or a dupatta tied into a bag
5 fruits and vegetables from the kitchen, for example a lemon, an onion, a banana, a tomato and a carrot

schedule.what: Guess five fruits and vegetables by touch. Then pick one to eat today.

activities.record: Draw the one that was hardest to guess.

setup.art: A grown-up putting a lemon, an onion, a banana, a tomato and a carrot into a cloth pillow cover, while a child covers their eyes.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up puts five foods in the bag.

setup.art: A child with one hand inside a cloth bag, eyes looking up, thinking hard.
setup.caption: 2. Feel one food. Say what you feel. Guess what it is.

flow.do: 1. Put the five foods in the bag while your child is not looking. 2. Your child puts one hand in and feels one food. 3. They say what they feel, then guess, then pull it out. 4. Do the same for each food.
flow.say: Put your hand in the bag. Hold one thing. Is it smooth or bumpy? Hard or soft? What do you think it is?
flow.kid: Feel one thing in the bag. Is it smooth or bumpy? Hard or soft? Guess!

good: Long and hard at one end.

flow.parent: Ask for describing words before the guess. A lemon has bumpy skin, a tomato is smooth and gives a little when pressed, an onion has dry papery skin.

flow.do: 1. Line up the five foods. 2. Ask which one your child thinks has the most water inside. 3. Ask which ones we eat raw and which we cook. 4. Let your child pick one to eat or cook with today.
flow.say: Which of these do you think has the most water inside? Which do we eat raw? Which do we cook? Which one would you like to eat today?
flow.kid: Which one has the most water inside? Which do we eat raw? Pick one to eat today.
flow.parent: Children often eat more of a food they have touched and chosen themselves.

activities.title: Make Kosambari: a crunchy salad from Karnataka
activities.context: In this activity you help make kosambari, a salad of soaked moong dal, cucumber and carrot. It is made in Karnataka for festivals and everyday meals. You find out which parts are wet and which were dry before soaking.

materials.item: split yellow moong dal, soaked in water for 2 hours, and a few dry grains kept aside
a cucumber
a carrot
half a lemon, salt, and grated coconut if you have it
a bowl and a spoon

schedule.what: Soak the dal 2 hours before. Then make and eat the kosambari together.

activities.record: Draw your bowl of kosambari. Colour the parts that had water inside.

setup.art: A small cup of dry yellow moong dal next to a bowl of the same dal soaked and swollen in water.
setup.caption: 1. Soak the moong dal for 2 hours. Compare it with dry dal.

setup.art: A child stirring a bowl of yellow dal, green cucumber bits and orange grated carrot, while a grown-up squeezes a lemon.
setup.caption: 2. Mix the dal, cucumber and carrot. Add lemon and salt.

flow.do: 1. Show your child a few dry moong dal grains next to the soaked dal. 2. Let them press one of each between finger and thumb.
flow.say: Press a dry dal grain. Now press a soaked one. What is different? Where did the water go?
flow.kid: Press a dry dal. Press a soaked dal. Which is soft? Where did the water go?

good: The dal soaked up the water and got bigger.

flow.parent: Soaked dal is bigger and soft enough to squash. The water went inside the grains.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up chops the cucumber and grates the carrot. 2. Your child drains the dal and tips everything into the bowl. 3. Your child squeezes the lemon, adds a pinch of salt and stirs.
flow.say: I will do the cutting. You tip in the dal, squeeze the lemon and stir. Which of these is the wettest?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts. You tip, squeeze and stir. Which part is the wettest?
flow.parent: Keep knives and the grater with the grown-up. Add the salt just before eating, because salt draws water out of the cucumber and makes the salad soggy.

flow.do: Eat the kosambari together. Ask your child to name each part as they eat it.
flow.say: Let's eat. Which part is crunchy? Which part is juicy? Which part tastes sour?
flow.kid: Eat your salad! Which part is crunchy? Which is juicy? Which is sour?
flow.parent: If your child does not like one part, that is fine. They can taste a tiny bit and leave the rest.

activities.title: My Water Tumbler: drops on a chart
activities.context: In this activity you keep a chart for one day. Every time you drink water, you draw a drop. You also draw what you were doing when you felt thirsty.

materials.item: a sheet of paper and crayons
your own tumbler or bottle

schedule.what: Draw a drop for every drink of water, from morning to bedtime. Count them at night.

activities.record: Your chart of drops, with a small picture of what you were doing when you felt thirsty.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with a big tumbler drawn on it, and a child drawing a blue drop beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your tumbler at the top of the paper.

setup.art: The same sheet at bedtime, with seven blue drops and a small drawing of a child playing in the sun.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a drop every time you drink. Count them at night.

flow.do: 1. Help your child draw their tumbler at the top of a sheet. 2. Stick the sheet on the fridge or a wall.
flow.say: Today we will draw a drop each time you drink water. Let's stick the chart where you can reach it.
flow.kid: Draw your tumbler. Each time you drink water today, draw a drop.
flow.parent: Count a full tumbler or a good few gulps from a bottle as one drop.

flow.do: Each time your child drinks water, they draw a drop. When they say they are thirsty, ask what they were doing. They draw a small picture of it next to the drop.
flow.say: You're thirsty? What were you just doing? Draw it next to your drop.
flow.kid: Thirsty? Drink, then draw a drop. Draw what you were doing.
flow.wait: Draw the drops through the day.
flow.parent: Children usually feel thirsty after running about, after a hot walk, and after salty food.

flow.do: At bedtime, count the drops together. Look at the small drawings.
flow.say: How many drops did you draw today? When did you feel most thirsty?
flow.kid: Count your drops. When were you most thirsty?

ask.q: When did you feel most thirsty?

flow.parent: There is no right number. You will drink more on hot days. Food gives some water too.

games.title: Wet, Damp or Dry? A food sorting game
games.context: This is a sorting game about water in food. Each card names a food. Players decide if it is Wet, Damp or Dry, and the back of the card gives the answer.

items.b: Wet. A cucumber is about 95 parts water out of 100.

img.credit: Patricia Rose, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Wet. Watermelon is more than 90 parts water out of 100.

img.credit: Sindhu Haridas, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Wet. A tomato drips juice when you squeeze it.
Wet. Each segment is full of juice.

img.credit: Jeanene Arrington-Fisher, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Wet. It is a drink that grows inside a coconut.
Wet. Buttermilk is mostly water, with a little curd.
Wet. Milk is mostly water.
Wet. Curd is mostly water, held thick.
Damp. A banana is about three-quarters water, held in a soft paste.

img.credit: Sagnik Dutta Roy, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.b: Damp. The grains took in water in the pot.
Damp. Idlis are steamed, and hold water inside.
Damp. A fresh chapati holds some water, but less than rice.
Dry. A biscuit is baked until almost all the water is gone.
Dry. Roasting drives out the water.
Dry. Puffed rice is crisp and dry.
Dry. Groundnuts hold very little water.
Dry. Papad is dried in the sun before it is fried or roasted.
Dry. Raw rice grains are hard. They go soft only after cooking in water.

printables.title: Three baskets to draw on a big sheet
items: A blue basket with three drops on it: 'Wet: runs or drips, mostly water'
A green basket with one drop on it: 'Damp: soft, with some water held inside'
A brown basket with a cross on it: 'Dry: hard or crunchy, almost no water'

rules: Draw the three baskets on a big sheet. Mix the cards and put them face down in a pile.
Take turns. Turn over the top card and say the food. A grown-up can read the card aloud.
Say which basket it goes in, and why. Point to the basket.
The grown-up reads the back of the card. If you were right, put the card in that basket and make a tick for yourself on paper.
If you were wrong, say the right basket together and put the card there. No tick.
When the pile is empty, count the ticks. Most ticks wins. Then count the cards in each basket: which basket has the most?

setup.art: A big sheet on the floor with a blue, a green and a brown basket drawn on it, and a pile of food cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw three baskets. Mix the cards.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says 'Watermelon' over the blue basket.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card, say why, and put it in a basket.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards. 2. Draw the three baskets. 3. Mix the cards and stack them face down.
flow.say: This game is about water hiding in food. Wet foods run or drip. Damp foods are soft, with water held inside. Dry foods are hard or crunchy.
flow.kid: Wet foods run or drip. Damp foods are soft. Dry foods are hard or crunchy. Let's sort!

flow.do: Take turns to turn a card, say the food, point to a basket and say why. The grown-up reads the back aloud.
flow.say: Where does this one go? Why do you think so? Let's read the back.
flow.kid: Turn a card. Wet, damp or dry? Say why.

check.q: Which basket does roasted chana go in?
check.why: Roasting drives the water out of chana, so the chana is crunchy and dry.

flow.parent: If you did the squeeze test, remind your child what the cucumber and the biscuit did.

flow.do: Count the cards. Then ask which basket holds the foods that help most on a hot day.
flow.say: Which basket would you pick from on a hot day? Why?
flow.kid: On a hot day, which basket would you pick from? Why?

good: The wet basket, because those foods give you water.

games.title: Water Keeper: a bean counting game
games.context: In this game your cup of beans is the water in your body. Some cards make you lose water, and some help you get it back. Try to end with 5 to 12 beans in your cup: not too little water, and not too much.

items.f: You played in the hot sun.
items.b: You sweated. Take out 2 beans.

items.f: You ran round the building three times.
items.b: You sweated and breathed hard. Take out 2 beans.
Your breath took a little water. Take out 1 bean.
Water leaves your body when you wee. Take out 1 bean.

items.f: You sat in a cool room and read a book.
items.b: You lost only a little water. Take out 1 bean.

items.f: You ate a bowl of salty chips.
items.b: Salt makes you thirsty. Take out 1 bean.

items.f: You walked to the market in the afternoon heat.
items.b: You sweated in the heat. Take out 2 beans.
You sweated and breathed hard. Take out 2 beans.

items.f: You drank a tumbler of water.
items.b: Put in 2 beans.

items.f: You drank a glass of buttermilk.
items.b: Put in 2 beans.
Put in 2 beans.
Put in 1 bean.

items.f: You ate a big piece of watermelon.
items.b: Put in 1 bean.
Put in 1 bean.
A biscuit has almost no water. No beans.

items.f: You ate a handful of roasted chana.
items.b: Roasted chana is dry. No beans.

rules: Each player has a cup or katori with 8 dried beans in it, like rajma. Put a heap of about 20 spare beans in the middle.
Mix the cards and stack them face down.
Take turns. Turn over a card. A grown-up reads it aloud, then reads the back.
Take out beans or put in beans, as the back says. If your cup is empty, you cannot take out any more.

If you have 4 beans or fewer, say 'I'm thirsty!' On your next turn, you may drink instead of reading a card: put in 2 beans from the heap. Then take the top card off the pile and put it aside without reading it.

Play until the cards run out. Everyone who ends with 5 to 12 beans had a comfortable day. With more than 12 beans, you drank too much. With fewer than 5, you were thirsty. Can everyone have a comfortable day?

setup.art: Three steel katoris, each with 8 rajma beans, and a heap of spare beans in the middle of a table, with a stack of cards.
setup.caption: 1. Put 8 beans in each cup. Stack the cards.

setup.art: A child turning over a card that shows a sun, and taking 2 beans out of her katori.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card. Take out or put in beans.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a cup with 8 beans. 2. Explain that the beans stand for the water in your body.
flow.say: Your beans are the water in your body. Some things make you lose water. Some things give it back.
flow.kid: Your beans are your body's water. Try to end with 5 to 12 beans in your cup!

flow.do: Play the cards in turn. After each card, ask how the water got in or out.
flow.say: You played in the sun. How did the water leave your body?
flow.kid: Read your card. Take out or put in beans. How did the water move?

check.q: A player ate a biscuit. How many beans do they put in?
check.why: A biscuit is dry. It gives you food, but almost no water.

flow.parent: The bean numbers are made up for the game. The idea is real: water leaves the body all day, and drinks and wet foods bring it back.

flow.do: At the end, ask which cards took the most water away, and which brought the most back.
flow.say: Which cards made you lose the most water? Which gave the most back?
flow.kid: Which cards took the most water? Which gave the most back?

ask.q: Which cards gave the most back?
good: The drinks: water, buttermilk and coconut water.

projects.title: Ten Tiny Tastes: can I learn to like a food?
projects.context: In this project you pick one food you do not like yet. For ten days, you taste a tiny bit of it, as small as a pea. You colour a face each day to show how it tasted.

materials.item: one food your family often eats that your child does not like yet, for example karela, bhindi, raw tomato, curd or a green vegetable
a sheet of paper with 10 empty circles drawn on it
crayons

schedule.what: Pick the food. Draw 10 circles. Taste a pea-sized bit and draw a face in circle 1.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 2.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 3.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 4.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 5.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 6.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 7.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 8.
Taste a tiny bit again. Draw a face in circle 9.
Taste for the tenth time. Draw the last face. Look at all ten faces together.

projects.record: The ten faces, one for each taste.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with ten empty circles in two rows, and a small steel spoon holding a pea-sized piece of cooked karela.
setup.caption: 1. Draw ten circles. Put a tiny bit of the food on a spoon.

setup.art: The same sheet with faces drawn in the circles: frowning faces at the start, then flat faces, then a small smile in the last circle.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, taste and draw a face. Look at how the faces change.

flow.do: 1. Let your child pick one food they do not like yet, from your usual meals. 2. Draw 10 circles together. 3. Put a pea-sized bit on a spoon. 4. Your child tastes it and draws a face in circle 1.
flow.say: Pick a food you don't like yet. Just taste a bit as small as a pea. You don't have to eat more.
flow.kid: Pick a food you don't like yet. Taste a tiny bit. Then draw a face.
flow.parent: Never push, bribe or praise heavily for eating it. Leann Birch found that pressure can make children like a food less. Spitting it into a napkin is allowed. The tasting is the whole job.

flow.do: Give a pea-sized taste at a calm moment, for example at the start of a meal. Your child draws a face in the next circle.
flow.say: Here is today's tiny taste. How was it? Draw your face.
flow.kid: Taste a tiny bit. How was it? Draw a face.
flow.wait: Taste again every day, on days 2 to 9.
flow.parent: Serve the food the same way each time, so the taste is the same. It is fine to eat it alongside a food your child likes.

flow.do: 1. Give the tenth taste. 2. Draw the last face. 3. Look at all ten faces in a row.
flow.say: Look at your ten faces. Did they change? Why do you think they changed, or stayed the same?
flow.kid: Look at your ten faces. Did they change? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the faces changed?
good: My tongue got used to it.
It didn't taste so strange any more.

ask.q: And if they did not change?
good: Maybe I just don't like it, and that is fine too.

flow.parent: Many children's faces go from frowning to flat over ten tastes, and some reach a smile. Some do not change, and that is a real result too. Everyone has a few foods they never come to like.

challenges.title: A Tiffin for a Hot School Day
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. On a hot day at school, there is no fridge, and you get thirsty. Can you plan a tiffin that helps?
challenges.problem: Plan a tiffin for a hot day. It must give you food so you can play, some water inside the food, and a drink. It must stay fresh until lunch without a fridge.
constraints: Use foods your family has at home.
It must include one wet food and one drink.
It must be something you like to eat.
general: Pack curd rice and a few cucumber slices, with a bottle of water.
Pack an orange or a few pieces of watermelon, with idli or chapati.
Fill the water bottle to the top, so you have plenty for the day.
creative: Freeze a half-full bottle of water overnight, then fill it up in the morning. It stays cold for hours and keeps the tiffin cool too.
Wrap the bottle in a wet cotton cloth. As the water dries off the cloth, the bottle stays cooler.
Pack a bottle of lemon water with a pinch of salt and a little sugar, for a drink that tastes good and replaces some of the water you sweat out.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own tiffin. Draw it. Pack it on a real day, and see if it worked by lunchtime.

setup.art: A child drawing a round tiffin box with three sections on paper, with cucumber, curd rice and an orange drawn inside.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your tiffin. Put in one wet food.

setup.art: An open steel tiffin with curd rice, cucumber slices and orange pieces, next to a water bottle wrapped in a damp cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Pack it on a real day. Was it still good at lunch?

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask your child what goes wrong with a tiffin on a hot day.
flow.say: On a hot day at school, what goes wrong with a tiffin? What do you need most?
flow.kid: On a hot day, what goes wrong with a tiffin? What do you need?

good: I finish my water too soon.

flow.do: Your child draws a tiffin with one wet food, one other food and a drink. Ask why they chose each one.
flow.say: Draw your tiffin. Which food has water inside? Why did you pick it?
flow.kid: Draw your tiffin. Put in one wet food and a drink. Why those?
flow.parent: Curd rice, idli and fruit keep well for a few hours. Very milky or creamy foods, and buttermilk, spoil faster in the heat.

flow.do: Pack the planned tiffin on a real day. Afterwards, ask how it was.
flow.say: Was your tiffin still good at lunch? Was your water cool? What would you change?
flow.kid: Was your tiffin good at lunch? What would you change?
flow.wait: Pack it on a real school or outing day.

worksheets.title: Water in food, and in me

items.p: Colour the wet foods blue. Colour the dry foods brown.
items.why: Cucumber, watermelon and orange are full of water, so they drip when squeezed. Biscuit, murmura and papad are dried or baked, so they hold almost no water.
items.art: Six small pictures: a cucumber, a biscuit, a slice of watermelon, a heap of murmura, an orange and a papad.

items.p: Draw the squeeze test. Draw the hanky, the glass, and what dripped out.
items.a: A twisted hanky over a glass, with drops falling from it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the food inside the hanky and the drops falling into the glass.
items.art: An empty box with a small glass drawn at the bottom.

items.p: Dry rice grains are hard. Cooked rice is soft. Where did the water in cooked rice come from?
items.why: The grains take in water as they cook in the pot. That is why they swell and go soft.

items.p: A biscuit gives your body as much water as a cucumber.
items.why: False. A biscuit is baked until almost all the water is gone. A cucumber is mostly water.

items.p: Three of these drip water when you squeeze them. Which one does not?
items.why: Roasted chana has been heated until almost all the water left. The other three are full of juice.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: why do we need to drink more water on a hot day?
items.a: On a hot day we sweat more, so more water leaves our body. We drink more to put it back.
items.why: A strong answer says that water leaves the body as sweat, and that drinking puts it back.

items.p: Meena, a girl of 6 in Kochi, has just eaten two small pieces of watermelon. It is a hot afternoon. Her grandmother is with her.

views.says: I don't need a drink of water now. The watermelon was full of water.
The watermelon helped. But on a hot day you still need a proper drink of water.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example: 'Grandmother, because a hot day takes a lot of water out of you.' Then it is fair to the other side: Meena is right that the watermelon gave her water.
items.why: Both are partly right. Watermelon really does give water. But a few pieces of fruit may not put back all the water lost on a hot day, and thirst tells you when you need more.

items.p: Here are the six foods from the squeeze test. Write W under each food that dripped. Write D under each food that stayed dry.
items.a: W under cucumber and watermelon. D under banana, cooked rice, biscuit and roasted chana.
items.why: Cucumber and watermelon dripped. The others did not drip. Banana and rice left a small damp mark on paper, but they hardly dripped.
items.art: Six foods in a row with an empty box under each: cucumber, watermelon, banana, cooked rice, biscuit, roasted chana.

items.p: Draw one thing you ate or drank today that had water in it.
items.a: Any food or drink with water, such as a cucumber, fruit, curd, buttermilk or rice.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a real food or drink from today, and the child can say where the water is.
items.art: An empty box with a small tumbler drawn at the corner.

items.p: Your mouth is dry and you want a drink. What is your body telling you?
items.why: A dry mouth and wanting a drink is thirst. Thirst is the body asking for water.

items.p: Put these in order, from the most water inside to the least: banana, biscuit, watermelon.
items.why: Watermelon is more than 90 parts water out of 100. Banana is about three-quarters water. A biscuit has almost none.

items.p: A cook leaves cut cucumber slices on a plate in the hot sun all day. By evening they are small and dry. Where did their water go?
items.why: Heat and moving air carry water away from the slices into the air. The water goes as vapour, which is water in bits too small to see. This is how foods like papad are dried too.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: your body needs food and it needs water. Why is food alone not enough?
items.a: Food helps me grow and move, but my body also loses water all day. Dry food does not put that water back.
items.why: A strong answer says that the body loses water all the time, and that many foods do not give enough water to replace it.

items.p: Two sisters in Bhubaneswar, Lipi aged 7 and Rina aged 5, are at dinner. There is karela on the table.

views.says: I will never like karela. It is too bitter.
I didn't like it either. Then I tasted a little bit lots of times. Now it is fine.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other sister has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For example: 'Lipi, because tasting many times helps people like a food.' Then it is fair to the other side: Rina is right that karela is very bitter, and some people never like it.
items.why: Scientists found that many children come to like a food after tasting it many times. But tongues differ, and some people keep disliking a food. Both views have some truth.

items.p: Some foods got their water from the plant. Some got it in the cooking pot. Sort them.
items.why: Cucumber, orange and coconut water held water when they grew. Rice, dal and idli batter are made from dry grains, and take in water when they are soaked and cooked.
items.art: Six small pictures: a cucumber, a bowl of rice, an orange, an idli, a coconut with a straw, and a bowl of dal.

items.p: You drew a drop each time you drank water. You drew 2 drops in the morning, 1 at lunch and 2 after playing. How many drops is that?
items.why: 2 and 1 make 3. 3 and 2 more make 5 drops.
items.art: A chart with a tumbler at the top and five blue drops in three groups.

items.p: Here is a picture of a child. Draw an arrow at each place where water leaves the body.
items.a: An arrow at the skin, for sweat. An arrow at the mouth and nose, for breath. Going to the toilet is a third way.
items.why: Water leaves the body as sweat through the skin, as water in the breath, and as wee.
items.art: An outline of a child standing, with space around for arrows.

items.p: Draw where the water in a cucumber came from, before the plant drank the water.
items.a: Rain falling on the ground, soaking into the soil, and going up the roots of the cucumber plant.
items.why: A strong drawing shows rain, soil, roots and the cucumber, in that order.
items.art: An empty box with a cucumber plant drawn at the right-hand side.

items.p: Cooked rice has water inside it.
items.why: True. The grains took in water in the cooking pot, and that is why they are soft.

items.p: Which of these drinks has no sugar added?
items.why: Plain water has no sugar. Rose milk has sugar stirred in, and most packet juices have sugar added or are naturally very sweet.

videos.title: A slow-motion or close-up video of water inside a cucumber or watermelon
videos.why: Shows how juicy plant foods hold water in tiny cells.
videos.check: Find a real, accurate close-up video. Check it does not claim exact numbers it cannot show.

videos.title: Why do we get thirsty? A short explainer for children
videos.why: Shows that the body loses water all day and that thirst asks for more.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why do we get Thirsty? | #aumsum #kids #education #science" by It's AumSum Time, 5 minutes, 29 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Cavities with Dr. Binocs: how sweet things harm teeth

videos.check: Found by search: "Cavities - The Dr. Binocs Show | Best Learning Videos For Kids | Peekaboo Kidz" by Peekaboo Kidz, 4 minutes, 42 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Why does your body need food?
opts: Only to make your tummy full
quiz.why: Food gives your body what it needs to grow, move and mend itself. Fullness and taste are part of eating, but they are not why your body needs food.

quiz.p: Water leaves your body all day. Which of these is one way it leaves?
quiz.why: Water leaves as sweat through your skin, in your breath, and when you go to the toilet.

quiz.p: In the Squeeze Test, the biscuit stayed dry when you squeezed it. Why?
opts: It is baked until almost all the water is gone
The hanky soaked up the water
It was not squeezed hard enough
quiz.why: Baking drives the water out of a biscuit. That is what makes it crunchy.

quiz.p: When do you need to drink the most water?
opts: On a cool day, sitting still
On a hot day, after running about
Just after waking up from a nap in a cool room
quiz.why: On a hot day, and when you run about, you sweat more. So more water leaves your body.

quiz.p: A child did not like curd rice the first time they tried it. What might help them like it?
opts: Never giving it to them again
Tasting a little many times, without being pushed
Making them finish a big bowl
quiz.why: Many children come to like a food after tasting it many times. Pushing them to eat it can make them like it less.

quiz.p: Tiny living beings called bacteria live in your mouth. What do they make from sugar?
opts: An acid that can harm your teeth
quiz.why: The bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar and make acid. The acid can make holes in teeth over time.

quiz.p: Some of the water your body needs comes inside your food.
quiz.why: True. Watery foods like cucumber, fruit, curd and cooked rice all give your body water.

quiz.p: Eating many kinds of food, with plenty of vegetables and fruit, helps keep your body healthy.
quiz.why: True. Different foods help your body in different ways, so a mix of many kinds works best.

quiz.p: Before the Squeeze Test, you guessed that banana was dry. Then the banana made a damp mark on paper. What should you say?
opts: My guess was wrong. The banana has some water inside.
Bananas are dry, whatever the test shows.
quiz.why: A good scientist changes their idea when the test shows something new. The damp mark showed the banana has water.

quiz.p: You feel thirsty. What is the best thing to do?
quiz.why: Thirst is your body asking for water. A biscuit has almost no water in it.

applications: Families keep water in clay pots in summer, because water seeping through the clay dries off the outside and keeps the water cool.
Doctors give water with a little salt and sugar to people who have lost a lot of water from a tummy upset.
Farmers and cooks know which vegetables keep well and which wilt fast, because of how much water they hold.
Dentists teach children to rinse their mouths after sweets, to wash the sugar off their teeth.

spotted.text: Cucumber slices with salt and chilli powder, sold at railway stations and bus stands on hot days.
spotted.art: A vendor's tray of cucumber slices sprinkled with red chilli powder at a railway platform.

spotted.text: Tender coconut sellers at the roadside, cutting open green coconuts full of coconut water.
spotted.art: A roadside cart heaped with green tender coconuts, and a seller cutting the top off one.

spotted.text: Buttermilk, called neer mor in Tamil Nadu and majjige in Karnataka, given out free at street stalls in summer.
spotted.art: A street stall with a big clay pot of buttermilk and steel tumblers lined up in a row.

spotted.text: Watermelons piled high on carts in April and May.
spotted.art: A handcart piled with dark green watermelons, with one cut open to show the red inside.

spotted.text: A clay matka or paanai of drinking water in a kitchen corner, with a tumbler on top.
spotted.art: A round clay pot on a stand in a kitchen corner, with a steel tumbler upside down on its lid.

open_questions.q: How does thirst go away so quickly when we drink?
open_questions.why_open: Thirst fades within a minute of drinking, before the water has reached the blood. Scientists studying mice have found brain cells that quieten as soon as water is swallowed. How exactly the body knows that water is on its way is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why do some people love a taste that others cannot stand?
open_questions.why_open: Genes, family meals and how often we taste a food all play a part. Nobody knows yet how much each one matters.

open_questions.q: What does thirst feel like to other living beings, such as a crow, an ant or a plant?
open_questions.why_open: Every living being needs water, and senses when they are short of it. A drooping plant and a panting crow are both showing that they need water. What it feels like from the inside, nobody knows.

ask_kids: Which food on your plate today has the most water inside?
When did you last feel thirsty? What were you doing?
Is there a food you did not like before, but like now?
Where do you think the water in a watermelon came from?
Why do you think we feel more thirsty after salty food?

jokes.j: What do you call a sad strawberry?
Why did the orange stop rolling?
Why did the banana go to the doctor?
Why did the biscuit go to the doctor?
Why did the tomato lose the race?
What do clouds wear under their raincoats?
Why did the cow go to space?

maths.problem: In the squeeze test, 6 foods were tested. 2 foods dripped water. How many did not drip?
maths.explain: Start with 6 foods. Take away the 2 that dripped. 4 are left. Those 4 were damp or dry.
maths.context: This is about the squeeze test, where you squeezed six foods in a hanky.
maths.why_maths: Counting how many foods dripped and how many did not shows how many of our foods are juicy.

maths.problem: You drank 3 tumblers of water on a cool day and 6 tumblers on a hot day. On which day did you drink more? How many more?
maths.answer: The hot day. You drank 3 more tumblers.
maths.explain: 6 is more than 3. Count on from 3 to 6: 4, 5, 6. That is 3 more. On hot days we sweat more, so we drink more.
maths.context: This is about the water tumbler chart, where you draw a drop for each drink.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two days shows that the weather changes how much water a body needs.

maths.problem: In the Wet, Damp or Dry game, there are 8 cards in the Wet basket, 4 in Damp and 6 in Dry. Which basket has the most cards?
maths.explain: 8 is more than 6, and 6 is more than 4. So Wet has the most, then Dry, then Damp.
maths.context: This is about the Wet, Damp or Dry sorting game.
maths.why_maths: Counting the cards in each basket shows which basket got the most foods.

maths.problem: In Ten Tiny Tastes, you drew a frown on days 1 to 4, a flat face on days 5 to 8, and a smile on days 9 and 10. Which faces did you draw most often?
maths.answer: The frown and the flat face, 4 times each. The smile came 2 times.
maths.explain: Days 1, 2, 3, 4 make 4 frowns. Days 5, 6, 7, 8 make 4 flat faces. Days 9 and 10 make 2 smiles. The faces changed as the tastes went on.
maths.context: This is about the Ten Tiny Tastes project, where you taste a tiny bit of one food for ten days.
maths.why_maths: Counting each kind of face shows whether a taste changed over the ten days.

founder: ideas/by_topic/food-and-a-balanced-diet.md: the SCI Cards for Barry Marshall and M. S. Swaminathan. Both were kept for higher levels, because their stories (stomach bacteria, high-yield farming) are beyond Class 1. The founder's oneness line ('the food on a plate was sunlight, soil, rain, bees and someone's work', PHILOSOPHY.md) shaped the roots thread.

Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, 1.4 Healthy food and drink: healthy lunch box, a healthy plate, drinking lots of water. This unit keeps those ideas but builds the investigation round water in food.
science: Water content of foods: cucumber about 95%, watermelon about 91 to 92%, banana about 75%, cooked white rice about 68 to 70%, biscuits a few percent (USDA FoodData Central; Indian Food Composition Tables, National Institute of Nutrition, Hyderabad, 2017).
Food supplies roughly 20 to 30% of daily water intake in adults (European Food Safety Authority, Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for Water, 2010).
Body water: about 60% of an adult's body weight, a little more in children. Water is lost through skin, breath, urine and faeces.
No evidence supports 8 glasses a day for everyone: H. Valtin, 'Drink at least eight glasses of water a day. Really?', American Journal of Physiology, 2002.
Sugar and behaviour: M. Wolraich, D. Wilson and J. White, 'The effect of sugar on behavior or cognition in children: a meta-analysis', JAMA, 1995, found no effect.
Newborns accept sweet and reject bitter tastes: J. E. Steiner, studies of facial expressions in newborn infants, 1970s.

Repeated exposure: L. L. Birch and D. W. Marlin, 'I don't like it, I never tried it: effects of exposure on two-year-old children's food preferences', Appetite, 1982. Pressure to eat reduces liking: Birch's later work and reviews. Leann Birch, 1946 to 2019, University of Illinois, then Penn State (from 1992).
Coriander tasting of soap linked partly to the smell receptor gene OR6A2: N. Eriksson and others, 2012.
Thirst is quenched before blood changes: C. A. Zimmerman and others (Zachary Knight's lab), Nature, 2016, in mice.
Kamala Sohonie's work on neera, the sap of palm trees, and its vitamins, for which she received the Rashtrapati Award.

Taittiriya Upanishad 3.2 (Bhrigu Valli): Bhrigu understood that food is Brahman, for from food beings are born, by food they live, and into food they return. Thirukkural 12: rain makes the food that people eat, and is itself a drink.

roots.context: In the Squeeze Test, water dripped out of a cucumber, and we found that some foods are mostly water. Now we ask what that tells us about our bodies, and about the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Squeeze Test, cucumber and watermelon dripped water when you squeezed them in a hanky, but the biscuit stayed dry. That water was inside the food all along. So eating a cucumber also gives your body a drink. Some of the water you need each day comes inside your food.
deep_truth.habit: We think of food and drink as two separate things. But a cucumber is mostly water, so eating a cucumber is partly drinking too.
deep_truth.evidence: In the squeeze test, cucumber and watermelon dripped water into the glass and made big wet marks on paper, while the biscuit and roasted chana gave no water at all.

three.who_am_i: More than half of your body is water. That water came in through your drinks and your food.
three.what_is_life: Every living being needs water. The cucumber plant drank water through their roots and kept it in their fruit.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water goes round and round: rain, the soil, a plant, a cucumber, you, the air, and rain again.

roots.thread: The water in a cucumber was rain once. The rain soaked into the soil. Then a cucumber plant stored that water in their fruit. You eat the cucumber, and the water becomes part of you. Then it leaves you in your sweat and breath, and rises to make clouds again.

teachings.teaching: The sage Bhrigu thought hard about where living beings come from. He understood that living beings are born from food, live by food, and go back into food.
teachings.link: Your body is built from what you eat and drink. Even the water in you came in through your food and your tumbler.

teachings.teaching: Rain grows the food that people eat. Rain is also a drink for them.
teachings.link: Rain grew the cucumber, and the water that drips from it is that rain.

science.text: A cucumber is about 95 parts water out of 100. The water is held in tiny living cells, and it keeps the cucumber firm and crisp.
When your body is short of water, a small part of your brain senses it and makes you feel thirsty. Exactly how thirst switches off so fast when you drink is still being studied.

other_view.view: Some doctors say a thirsty child should drink water first. A few slices of cucumber or watermelon hold much less water than a tumbler does.

practice.title: One slow bite
practice.say: Take one slice of cucumber. Hold it and feel how cool it is. Now take one small bite, and chew very slowly. Feel the water come out on your tongue. Close your eyes. This water was rain once. Then a cucumber plant drank this water. Now the water is becoming part of you.
practice.kid: Hold a cucumber slice. Feel how cool it is. Take one slow bite. Feel the water on your tongue. That water was rain once. Now it is part of you.

ask: When you eat a cucumber, are you eating or drinking?
The water in you was in a cucumber, and before that in the rain. Where will it go next?
Is the water in your body part of you, or just passing through?
roots.art: A child with eyes closed, taking a slow bite of a cucumber slice, with a faint picture of rain clouds and a cucumber vine behind them.

how_we_found_out.context: Can a child learn to like a food? This card tells the true story of a scientist who found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many grown-ups thought that a child who pushed away a new food simply did not like it, and never would. Others thought the answer was to make the child eat it. Leann Birch, an American scientist, decided to test these ideas. She studied how small children learn to eat, first at the University of Illinois and, from 1992, at Penn State University. In one study, she and David Marlin gave two-year-olds small tastes of foods that were new to them. Some foods were offered only a few times, and others many times. The more often a child had tasted a food, the more they came to like it. Birch also found that pushing children to eat a food could make them like it less. So the old idea was wrong. A first 'no' is often not a forever 'no'. Liking a food is something a child learns, one small taste at a time. Leann Birch died in 2019. Parents and doctors around the world still use what she found.
how_we_found_out.who: Leann Birch, an American scientist who studied how children learn to eat, with David Marlin
how_we_found_out.when: Her first tasting study with David Marlin was published in 1982. She went on studying children's eating until her death in 2019.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought that a child who dislikes a new food will always dislike it, or that making a child eat a food will make them like it. Birch showed that liking grows with many small tastes, and that pressure can make a child like a food less.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist kneeling at a low table with a small child, offering a tiny spoonful from one of several little bowls, with a notebook beside her.

playtest: Walked through every card, game and experiment as a parent and a Class 1 child would, in a city flat. Fixed the squeeze test so the paper test and the squeeze test use the same mashed food, the napkin count is explained, and the hanky is tightly woven. Made the sorting game end clearly with ticks and baskets that match the maths question, gave the bean game a spare heap and a rule for skipped cards, made the feely bag and day-one taste steps match their minutes and schedules, shortened the story and the explanation cards, removed repeated worksheet questions (sweets, sugar, 8 glasses), gave the jokes she/he instead of it, renamed a repeated name. The three videos still have no checked link, so they stay marked to find; I did not invent any.
